title: Extract All Numbers
prompt: Write `extract_digits(text)` using `re.findall` that returns a list of every digit-sequence found in `text`, as strings.
hint: re.findall(r'\d+', text) returns every run of one-or-more digits as a list of strings.
explanation: \d+ matches one or more consecutive digits; findall collects every non-overlapping match in the string.

title: Validate a Username
prompt: Write `is_valid_username(name)` using `re.fullmatch` that returns True if `name` consists only of letters, digits, and underscores, and is at least 1 character long.
hint: re.fullmatch requires the ENTIRE string to match, unlike search — use [A-Za-z0-9_]+ and wrap the result in bool(...).
explanation: fullmatch (not search or match) is essential here — search would accept 'bad name!' by finding a valid-looking substring inside it.

title: Extract Email Domain
prompt: Write `extract_domain(email)` using a capturing group that returns the domain part of a simple email address (everything after `@`), or `None` if the string doesn't match.
hint: re.fullmatch(r'[\w.]+@([\w.]+)', email) — the group captures everything after @; return m.group(1) if there's a match, else None.
solution:
import re
def extract_domain(email):
    m = re.fullmatch(r'[\w.]+@([\w.]+)', email)
    return m.group(1) if m else None
explanation: The capturing group isolates just the domain, so you don't need to manually split the string on '@' and handle the no-match case yourself.

title: Redact Phone Numbers
prompt: Write `redact_phone_numbers(text)` using `re.sub` that replaces any sequence matching `XXX-XXX-XXXX` (digits and dashes) with the literal text `'REDACTED'`.
hint: re.sub(r'\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}', 'REDACTED', text) replaces every match in one call.
explanation: {3} and {4} require an exact digit count, so this pattern won't accidentally match a differently-shaped number sequence.

title: Parse a Date String
prompt: Write `parse_date(date_str)` using named groups that returns `{'year': ..., 'month': ..., 'day': ...}` (as strings) parsed from a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string, or `None` if it doesn't match.
hint: re.fullmatch(r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})', date_str) — call .groupdict() on the match if it exists.
solution:
import re
def parse_date(date_str):
    m = re.fullmatch(r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})', date_str)
    return m.groupdict() if m else None
explanation: groupdict() turns the three named groups directly into the exact dict shape the function needs to return, with no manual key assignment.

title: Capstone: Log Parser
prompt:
Build a `LogParser` class that parses simple `'LEVEL: message'` log lines using a compiled, named-group regex pattern.

Implement:
- A class attribute `LINE_PATTERN` — a compiled regex matching `'LEVEL: message'` with named groups `level` and `message` (e.g. `r'(?P<level>\w+): (?P<message>.+)'`).
- `__init__(self)` — store an empty `entries` list.
- `parse_line(self, line)` — match `line` against `LINE_PATTERN`; if it matches, append `{'level': ..., 'message': ...}` to `entries` and return `True`; otherwise return `False` without appending anything.
- `count_by_level(self)` — return a dict counting how many entries exist per level.
- `find_messages_matching(self, pattern)` — return a list of messages (in insertion order) whose text matches the given regex `pattern` string.
- `summary(self)` — return `{'total': <entry count>, 'by_level': <count_by_level() result>}`.
hint: __init__ stores self.entries = []. parse_line uses LINE_PATTERN.match(line); if it returns None, return False; otherwise append m.group('level')/m.group('message') as a dict and return True. count_by_level can use collections.Counter over entry levels. find_messages_matching compiles the given pattern and filters entries whose message it matches with .search(). summary composes len(self.entries) and count_by_level().
explanation: This mirrors a real log-ingestion tool: a single compiled pattern (built once as a class attribute, not recompiled on every call) extracts structured fields from raw text, and the class builds simple aggregations (counts, filtered search) on top of the parsed records — the same shape as this topic's earlier lessons, combined into one stateful class.
